In 2023, very heavy rain fell on cocoa farms in West Africa, and black pod disease rotted the pods. Ghana’s farms harvested much less cocoa (from six hundred fifty-six thousand to five hundred thirty-one thousand tonnes). With less cocoa in the world, buyers paid much more for every tonne (from about two thousand four hundred to over ten thousand dollars a tonne). Grinding factories in Europe paid more for beans and ground less cocoa (least in four years). Chocolate makers paid more for cocoa, so they raised prices or made bars smaller (about ten percent or more). So rain in Ghana reached our store: shoppers here pay more or get less chocolate.

Cocoa farming is hard, and many families earn very little. In 2018-19 a study counted about 1.56 million children doing child labor in cocoa-growing areas of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Most of it was dangerous work, like using sharp machetes or carrying heavy loads. Ghana’s rules forbid dangerous work for children under 18.

Cacao trees first grew in South America, where people in what is now Ecuador used cacao more than 5,000 years ago. In Ghana, people honor Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith who brought cocoa pods home from the island of Fernando Po and started a farm at Mampong in 1879. Ghanaian farmers built it into one of the world’s biggest cocoa crops; missionaries had planted some trees earlier.
2023: very heavy rain fell on cocoa farms in West Africa. Black pod disease rotted many pods. A tree virus and illegal gold mining on farmland made it worse. The world’s cocoa harvest fell about 14%.
That is the price Ghana pays its farmers for a bag, not the world price for a tonne.

Akosua and Kwame Boateng grow cocoa on about 2 hectares, like many of Ghana’s roughly 800,000 cocoa families. They cut ripe pods by hand, ferment the beans under plantain leaves for about a week, and dry them in the sun. Their two children go to school.

Ghana harvested about 531,000 tonnes, down from about 656,000: about 1 bag in 5 lost. Ghana raised its farm price from GH¢800 a bag to GH¢1,308, then GH¢2,070. Fewer bags, more for each bag. The world price rose even faster, more than 4 times.
Yaw is a purchasing clerk. He weighs each bag and pays the price Ghana’s cocoa board sets (16 bags make a tonne). He sells the bags on to the board’s marketing company for export.
Fewer bags came in, so Yaw had less to weigh and buy.
Kojo loads cocoa onto ships at Takoradi. Most of Ghana’s cocoa leaves as beans for factories abroad.
In the first half of 2024, Ghana shipped less cocoa and earned less from cocoa sold abroad than a year earlier. Fewer bags means less loading work.
Sanne runs a grinder. The Netherlands brings in more cocoa beans than any other country; factories roast and grind them into cocoa butter, cocoa powder and cocoa paste for chocolate makers.
Beans cost over 4 times as much. Late in 2024, factories in Europe ground less cocoa than in any three months in 4 years. Less grinding can mean fewer shifts.
Luis works the line where chocolate fills bar moulds.
Cocoa cost far more. In 2025 a big US chocolate maker announced price rises of about 10% or more and smaller packs.
Dana runs the register.
Shoppers here pay more for a bar, or get a smaller one. Rain in Ghana reached this shelf.
